item.title: Comprehensive Survey: Remote Desktop and Remote Terminal Technologies
item.description: Operating one machine from another decomposes into three engineering problems: getting the remote screen to your display (rendering), sending your keyboard and mouse over (input), and establishing a channel between the two machines that survives NAT (connectivity). The first two produced RDP, VNC, and SSH; the third produced ID-based addressing, hole punching, and relay networks. This article maps the remote desktop and remote terminal landscape along these lines: the split between two rendering routes, the evolution of RDP’s graphics pipeline, the Wayland shake-up on Linux desktops, the connection logic of commercial products and RustDesk, the SSH ecosystem’s answers to disconnection, enterprise access layers, and the KVM-over-IP layer below the operating system.

item.title: A Detailed Comparison of Remote Access Products and Open-Source Projects
item.description: The two previous posts covered the technical landscape and the RDP protocol itself: A Comprehensive Survey of Remote Desktop and Remote Terminal Technologies gives the panorama, RDP Protocol Deep Dive goes down to the wire format. This post adds the selection perspective: it puts the industry’s well-known products and open-source projects against the same set of dimensions — connection architecture, codecs, encryption, self-hostability, license, activity, security incidents — table first, commentary after. Data time point is October 2026; GitHub stars and licenses were fetched via the GitHub API, product behavior comes from official documentation and security advisories, and no benchmark measurements are included.
